messages.subject: General Methodology Questions
parts:
Hello,

I am trying to learn the inner workings of INLA and the SPDE approach to spatial statistics. I have a couple methodology questions and I hope this is an okay place to ask them.

For now, I am just looking at the simple model

Y = X + epsilon

where X~N(0, Q(theta)^-1) are the spatial effects and epsilon is a random error term. My interest is in making inferences/predictions about X. I have two questions (or at least these are the two biggest right now :) ).

1) Is it reasonable in some scenarios to draw MCMC samples  from p(theta | Y) and use these for Monte Carlo integration to obtain p(X_i | Y)? I am trying to reach into the multivariate spatial setting, where 'theta' may contain p x p covariance matrices for p around 50. I am worried about the ability of quasi-Newton methods to explore this space, but potentially it won't be too difficult to draw samples from the distribution.

2) Now let's say I either have a batch of samples from p(theta|Y), or a set of points and weights from the quasi-Newton method, and want to make inferences about X_i. Do I just perform the numerical integration for some grid of X_i values for a numerical estimate of the posterior, or is there some more efficient way?

Cheers!
Paul

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] General Methodology Questions
parts:
Hi,

some brief thoughts:
1) Yes, doing the full INLA method with all those covariance parameters would be difficult, both in the optimisation and deterministic integration stages.
If the optimisation could find a reasonable mode, you could potentially use some form of importance sampling Monte Carlo integration with respect to theta, but likely the optimisation itself would be a problem, and mcmc needed to explore the posterior for theta.

2) This stage is much easier. In your example, the conditional posterior for X given theta is also Gaussian (if epsilon is Gaussian), so you can compute everything;
When you have samples theta_k ~ p(theta|Y), k=1,...,K, then
  \int p(X|\theta,Y) p(\theta|Y) d\theta
can be approximated by
  \sum_k p(X|\theta_k,Y) / K,
which describes a mixture of multivariate Gaussians, with mean and precision known.
The details will depend on what properties of that multivariate mixture you need.

Conditional Gaussian posteriors (see the 2005 Rue&Helf GMRF book):
  m_x = prior expectation for x
  Q_x = prior precision for x, conditionally on theta
  Q_e = prior precision for e, conditionally on theta
Linear observations for some sparse matrix A (basis function evaluations in SPDE/GMRF models, for example, but more generally the linear model design matrix):
  y = A x + e
Conditional Posterior, x|y,\theta:
  Q_{x|y,\theta} = Q_x + A' Q_e A
   m_{x|y,\theta} = mu_x + Q_{x|y,\theta}^{-1} A' Q_e (y - A m_x)

Now, if you need this for other observation likelihoods than Normal, but you have managed to sample from p(theta|Y), you can still in principle use the conditional Laplace approximation for integrating out components of x to get better marginal posteriors than just using the Hessian in the equations above.  Lots more details depending on the specific model/context, but hopefully that gives some food for thought!

Finn


Finn

parts:
I think I may be able to solve for the mode of the covariance matrices with respect to fixed Matern parameters in closed form, so maybe the optimization is reasonable. I will look into this, as well as a subsequent application of importance sampling.

Yes, I see now that my estimated posterior for X_i will indeed be linear combination of Gaussians with weights defined by my samples from p(\theta|Y). This is definitely the way to look at it :)

Thank you for your time. This was helpful to me.
